title: How do you deliver a 60-second recommendation at the end of a case?
description: The last 60 seconds are what the interviewer remembers and writes up. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Deliver a 60-second recommendation in four beats: the answer in one sentence, two or three reasons with numbers, the main risk, and the next steps, including anything you did not get to. Take about 20 seconds to prepare and then speak to the interviewer as if they were the CEO. The last minute is what the interviewer remembers and writes up, so make it short, clear and decisive.
body:
Stage 9 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why the last 60 seconds matter

The recommendation is the last thing the interviewer hears, and it shapes how they remember the whole case. It is also often the moment they test you hardest, by asking you to imagine the CEO walking in. The common mistake is replaying the case from the start ("First we looked at...") instead of giving the answer. This explainer gives you a script you can use every time; the full method, with a worked M&A example, is in how to give a strong recommendation.

The 60-second script

"I recommend [decision]. Two reasons: [reason with a number], and [reason with a number]. The main risk is [risk], which we'd manage by [mitigation]. As next steps, I'd [first action], and I'd also look at [branch we didn't cover]."

Four beats, in that order:

  1. Answer: one sentence, first. If it is conditional, the condition goes in the same sentence.
  2. Reasons: two or three, each with a number from the case.
  3. Risk: the one thing most likely to make you wrong, and how to manage it.
  4. Next steps: what to do on Monday, plus any part of your structure you never reached.

Prepare in 20 seconds

Ask: "May I take a moment to pull this together?" Then glance at the goal box at the top of your notes and jot one line per beat. Check two things before you speak: does the answer match the question that was actually asked, and does it hit the client's target? If it falls short, say by how much.

A worked example

At the end of the Coastal Brew case, you know:

  • Operating profit fell $7.5M, from $12M to $4.5M, while revenue rose $2M.
  • Delivery grew from 5% to 25% of sales, and a delivery order adds only about $0.45 of real profit once you account for the café visits it replaces.
  • Raising app menu prices 15% would add about $1.45M a year.
  • The target is at least $10M within two years, a gap of $5.5M.

Weak:

"So we started by looking at the P&L, and we saw that commissions had gone up a lot. Then we compared in-store and delivery orders, and delivery was less profitable. Then we brainstormed some ideas, and the price rise looked good..."

Strong:

"Coastal Brew's profit has fallen $7.5M because delivery has grown from 5% to 25% of sales, and a delivery order adds only about 45 cents of real profit once you allow for the café visits it replaces. I recommend three moves: raise app menu prices about 15%, worth roughly $1.45M a year; launch click-and-collect in our own app to move customers off the commission channels; and renegotiate commissions. The price rise closes about $1.45M of the $5.5M gap to the $10M target, so the rest has to come from the other two moves, which we should size next. The main risk is that the apps rank us lower in search. Next step: test the price rise in 10 stores for 4 weeks before rolling it out."

The strong version leads with the cause and the decision, puts numbers on both, admits the price rise alone does not reach the target and names a cheap test.

When the interviewer pushes back

After your recommendation, expect a challenge: "What if the apps refuse to lower commissions?" Do not abandon your answer, and do not dig in blindly. Acknowledge the point, say whether it changes the decision and adjust if needed:

"Then the price rise and click-and-collect become more important. If both together still fall short of $10M, I'd look at reducing our presence on the apps in stores where most delivery orders replace café visits."

A recommendation should not pretend uncertainty has gone. It should give the best-supported decision now and the test that would change it. "The client should analyse this further" without a choice is not a recommendation.

Common mistakes

  • Replaying the case. The answer comes first.
  • No numbers in the reasons. "Delivery is less profitable" is weaker than "a delivery order adds 45 cents".
  • Hiding a shortfall. If your levers do not reach the target, say so and say what comes next.
  • Forgetting what you did not cover. Unexplored branches go into next steps.
  • Running long. Past 90 seconds you are summarising, not recommending.

Practise the moment

Say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. The interviewer says: "The CEO walks in. What do you tell her?"

Show a strong answer

"I recommend X. Two reasons: [reason with a number], and [reason with a number]. The main risk is Y, so as next steps I'd Z."

Why it works: Answer first, reasons with numbers, risk, next steps, in about 60 seconds.

2. You never got to the cost side of your structure. Where does it go?

Show a strong answer

In next steps: "...and I'd also look at the cost side, which we didn't get to today."

Why it works: It shows you tracked the whole problem.

3. You found a market growing 12% a year, and a joint venture that caps the client's investment at $20M with break-even in year 2. The partner could walk away. Recommend.

Show a strong answer

"I recommend entering through a joint venture. Two reasons: the market grows 12% a year, and a partner caps our investment at $20M with break-even in year 2. The key risk is depending on the partner, so as next steps I'd agree exit terms up front and test demand in one city."

Why it works: It is decisive, evidenced and turns the main risk into a concrete next step.

Where to practise next

Take three finished cases from the casebook, read only the findings and give each recommendation out loud in under 60 seconds, timed. Drill the script with the flashcards on the perfect casing page. The final stage is the habits that matter throughout the case.
